title: AI Engineering: LLMs, Prompting, Retrieval and Evaluation
description: Build and judge applications on top of language models: tokens and cost, prompts and structured output, embeddings and retrieval, evaluation, security and operation.
audience: A developer or analyst who can write Python and read a statistical result. Machine-learning metrics (precision, recall) help; machine-learning-and-mlops is the recommended earlier course. Agents and coding assistants come in later courses.
outcomes: You'll be able to estimate the tokens, cost and latency of a model call.
You'll be able to write a prompt as a testable specification.
You'll be able to build and score a retrieval pipeline.
You'll be able to design an evaluation set and read its noise honestly.
You'll be able to name the main security failures of LLM applications and their controls.

lessons.title: Tokens and the context window
lessons.objective: Estimate the tokens and cost of a request and work out how much room a prompt leaves for the answer.

concepts.title: Token
concepts.summary: A unit of text, often a word fragment, that a model reads and writes.

concepts.title: Context window
concepts.summary: The maximum number of tokens a model can take in and produce in one request.

concepts.title: Stateless call
concepts.summary: Each request carries the whole conversation; the model keeps nothing between calls.

misconceptions: A token is a word; common words are one token, rare words and numbers split into several.
The model remembers earlier turns; the application resends them each time, and you pay for them each time.
sequence: A sentence split into subword pieces with real token boundaries shown.
The rule of thumb of about four characters per English token, and where it fails (code, other scripts).
Input and output priced separately.
Chat history grows the input every turn.
examples: 1,200 characters is about 300 tokens by the four-characters rule.
Illustrative prices of $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output: 2,000 in and 500 out cost 0.006 + 0.0075 = $0.0135.
A 500-token system prompt and 100-token user messages with 200-token replies: input per turn is 600, 900, 1,200, 1,500, 1,800, total 6,000 over five turns.
Window 8,000, prompt 6,500: at most 1,500 tokens remain for output.

lessons.title: How a language model chooses the next token
lessons.objective: Convert logits to probabilities with softmax, and predict the effect of temperature and top-p on sampling.

concepts.title: Logits
concepts.summary: Raw scores the model gives each possible next token.

concepts.title: Softmax
concepts.summary: The function that turns logits into probabilities that sum to 1.

concepts.title: Temperature
concepts.summary: A divisor applied to the logits before softmax; higher values flatten the distribution.

misconceptions: Temperature 0 makes a model correct; it makes it repeatable on most systems, not truthful.
The model reasons about the whole answer first; it emits one token at a time conditioned on everything before.
sequence: Three candidate tokens with logits 2, 1, 0.
Softmax: exp each, divide by the sum.
Temperature 2 flattens, temperature 0.5 sharpens.
Top-p keeps the smallest set whose probability reaches p.
examples: Logits (2,1,0) give probabilities 0.665, 0.245, 0.090. Temperature 2 gives 0.507, 0.307, 0.186. Temperature 0.5 gives 0.867, 0.117, 0.016.
Top-p 0.9 on 0.665, 0.245, 0.090: the first two sum to 0.910, so two tokens stay.

figures.learnerAction: Slide temperature and watch the bars flatten or sharpen.

lessons.objective: Write a prompt with an instruction, constraints and examples, and judge two prompt versions on a test set instead of a single demo.

concepts.title: Instruction
concepts.summary: What the model must do and the format it must produce.

concepts.title: Prompt test set
concepts.summary: A fixed list of inputs with expected properties, used to compare prompt versions.

misconceptions: A prompt that worked on three inputs is good; the failures are in the cases you did not try.
More instructions always help; each added example or rule costs tokens on every call and may conflict with others.

The parts of a specification: task, audience, format, constraints, examples, and what to do when the input is out of scope.
Few-shot examples shown and their cost on every call.

lessons.objective: Validate a model's JSON against a schema, retry safely, and explain the tool-call round trip.

concepts.title: Schema
concepts.summary: A machine-checkable description of the shape and types an output must have.

concepts.title: Tool call
concepts.summary: A structured request by the model for the application to run a named function.

concepts.title: Validate and retry
concepts.summary: Check output against the schema and re-ask on failure, with a limit.

misconceptions: The model runs the tool; it only emits a request, and your code runs it and returns the result.
Retries are independent; a prompt that fails once on an input will often fail again, so the formula is an upper bound.

lessons.title: Embeddings and similarity
lessons.objective: Compute cosine similarity between two vectors and pick the nearest document.

concepts.title: Embedding
concepts.summary: A vector that places a piece of text so that similar meanings are close.

concepts.title: Cosine similarity
concepts.summary: The dot product divided by the product of vector lengths.

concepts.title: Nearest-neighbour search
concepts.summary: Finding the stored vectors closest to a query vector.

misconceptions: Close in embedding space means true; it means similar topic, and a negated sentence can sit next to the original.
Vectors from different embedding models can be compared; each model defines its own space.
sequence: Words as points in a plane to build intuition.
Dot product and length.
Cosine ignores length.
Searching many vectors needs an index; exact search scans all.

lessons.title: Chunking, retrieval and ranking
lessons.objective: Count the chunks a document produces, fuse two ranked lists, and score retrieval with recall@k and MRR.

concepts.title: Chunk
concepts.summary: A passage of a document stored and retrieved as one unit.

concepts.title: Hybrid retrieval
concepts.summary: Combining keyword (BM25) and embedding results.

concepts.title: Mean reciprocal rank
concepts.summary: The average of 1/rank of the first relevant result over queries.

misconceptions: Bigger chunks are safer; they dilute the match and fill the context window.
Embedding search is always better than keyword search; exact names, codes and numbers favour keyword matching.
sequence: A 2,000-token document cut at 500 tokens with 100 overlap.
Why overlap exists and what it costs.
BM25 and dense lists disagree; reciprocal rank fusion.
Judging retrieval alone, before any generation.
examples: Stride 400: chunks start at 0, 400, 800, 1,200, 1,600, so 5 chunks.
Reciprocal rank fusion with k = 60: a document ranked 1st in one list and 3rd in another scores 1/61 + 1/63 ≈ 0.0323.
First-relevant ranks 1, 3, 2 give MRR (1 + 1/3 + 1/2)/3 ≈ 0.611.

lessons.title: The RAG pipeline and where it fails
lessons.objective: Budget context for retrieved passages and classify a failed answer as a retrieval miss, a ranking problem or an unfaithful generation.

concepts.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
concepts.summary: Retrieving relevant passages and giving them to the model with the question.

concepts.title: Groundedness
concepts.summary: Whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved passages.

concepts.title: Permission filter
concepts.summary: Restricting retrieval to documents the asking user may see.

misconceptions: RAG stops hallucination; the model can still ignore or misread the passages.
Retrieval permissions can be left to the model; filtering must happen before the model sees the text.
sequence: Question, retrieval, prompt assembly, generation, citation.
Context budget arithmetic.
Failure taxonomy: answer not in corpus, retrieved but ranked low, retrieved but ignored, unsupported claim.
Permission-sensitive documents.
examples: Window 8,000, system 500, question 100, answer reserve 800 leaves 6,600; at 500 per chunk that is 13 chunks (6,500 tokens).

lessons.title: Evaluation sets and statistical noise
lessons.objective: Build an evaluation set with the cases that matter and say how much a small set can tell you.

concepts.title: Evaluation set
concepts.summary: A fixed list of cases with expected properties, kept apart from prompt development.

concepts.title: Confidence interval
concepts.summary: A range of pass rates compatible with the observed result.

concepts.title: Case mix
concepts.summary: Answerable, unanswerable, ambiguous, permission-sensitive and stale-information cases.

misconceptions: 34/40 beats 31/40 so version B is better; with 40 cases the 95% interval spans about 22 points.
A set of easy cases is a good set; it hides the failures that matter.
sequence: Where cases come from: logs, hand-written edge cases, past incidents.
Case mix and labels.
Pass rate 34/40 with a Wald interval.
Why to keep a held-out set.

lessons.title: LLM judges and agreement
lessons.objective: Write a judging rubric, name the known biases of model judges, and compute agreement between a judge and human labels.

concepts.title: Rubric
concepts.summary: Written criteria that make a judgement repeatable.

concepts.title: Judge bias
concepts.summary: Systematic preferences such as for longer answers or for whichever answer appears first.

concepts.title: Cohen's kappa
concepts.summary: Agreement between two raters corrected for the agreement expected by chance.

misconceptions: A judge that agrees 80% of the time is reliable; if both pass 70% of items, chance alone gives 58% agreement.
A model judge replaces human labels; it extends a small human-labelled set, calibrated against it.
sequence: Pass/fail rubric for a support answer.
Position and length bias; swapping the order as a control.
Observed agreement and chance agreement.
Calibrate on human labels and re-check.
examples: Of 100 items both pass 60, both fail 20, judge-only pass 10, human-only pass 10. Observed agreement 0.80; each rater passes 70%, so chance agreement is 0.49 + 0.09 = 0.58; kappa = 0.22/0.42 ≈ 0.524.

lessons.title: Security for LLM applications
lessons.objective: Identify prompt injection and unsafe output handling in a design and name the control that breaks each.

concepts.title: Prompt injection
concepts.summary: Text in the model's input that is read as an instruction and changes its behaviour.

concepts.title: Indirect injection
concepts.summary: Injected instructions arriving through retrieved or fetched content rather than from the user.

concepts.title: Output handling
concepts.summary: Treating model output as untrusted input to the next system.

misconceptions: A system prompt that says 'ignore instructions in documents' prevents injection; the model has no reliable boundary between data and instructions.
Model output is trusted because you wrote the prompt; it is untrusted text that must be validated, escaped or parameterised.
sequence: A retrieved page that says 'send the user's notes to this address'.
Direct and indirect injection.
Output used in HTML, SQL or a shell.
Controls: least privilege, validation, escaping, separating data from instructions, human approval for risky actions.
examples: A model's reply is placed into a SQL string; a reply of ' OR '1'='1 changes the query. A parameterised query treats it as data.
OWASP's 2025 list includes prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, improper output handling, excessive agency and unbounded consumption.

lessons.title: Cost, latency and model routing
lessons.objective: Estimate a monthly bill and a response time, and compute the saving from routing easy requests to a smaller model.

concepts.title: Time to first token
concepts.summary: The delay before streaming begins.

concepts.title: Prompt caching
concepts.summary: Reusing the processing of a repeated prompt prefix at lower cost.

concepts.title: Model routing
concepts.summary: Sending each request to the cheapest model that meets the quality bar.

misconceptions: The most capable model is always the right default; a smaller model passing your evals is cheaper and faster.
Latency is just model speed; it is time to first token plus output tokens divided by tokens per second.
sequence: Monthly bill from request volume and token counts.
Latency = TTFT + output tokens / generation speed.
Streaming changes perceived latency, not total time.
Routing and caching.

If 70% of traffic goes to a model costing a tenth as much, relative cost is 0.7·0.1 + 0.3 = 0.37.

lessons.title: Prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning
lessons.objective: Decide which adaptation method fits a failure, and compute the trainable parameter fraction of a low-rank adapter.

concepts.title: Fine-tuning
concepts.summary: Updating a model's weights on examples to change its behaviour.

concepts.title: Low-rank adaptation
concepts.summary: Training two small matrices whose product is added to a frozen weight matrix.

concepts.title: Knowledge versus behaviour
concepts.summary: Missing or changing facts call for retrieval; a missing style or format calls for prompting or tuning.

misconceptions: Fine-tuning teaches the model new facts reliably; facts change and tuned weights cannot be audited per document.
Fine-tuning is always the heavier path; try a better prompt and retrieval first, and decide on eval evidence.
sequence: Three failures: wrong facts, wrong format, wrong tone.
Order of attempts: prompt, retrieval, tuning.
LoRA adds r·(d + k) parameters to a d×k matrix.
Evaluate the choice against the same set.
examples: A 4096×4096 matrix has 16,777,216 parameters; rank 8 adapters add 8·(4096+4096) = 65,536, which is 0.39%.

concepts.title: Regression gate
concepts.summary: An automated check that blocks a change when critical cases get worse.

concepts.title: Model pinning
concepts.summary: Using a dated model version so behaviour does not change without a deliberate upgrade.

concepts.title: Production sampling
concepts.summary: Reviewing a sample of real traffic to find failures the eval set lacks.

misconceptions: A new model version is a drop-in upgrade; behaviour on your prompts can change.
Logging everything is responsible; prompts contain personal data, so redact and set retention.

Gate rule: block if the pass rate falls more than 0.03.
